transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-12-09 10:30 PST — Duration approx 52 minutes. Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendez (CTO — Salix), Priya Kapoor (Lead ML Eng — Salix), Sofia Lane (Platform Eng — Salix).

Summary: weekly pilot convergence check — focus on latency/throughput deltas versus incumbent vendor, routing and quantization knobs, and next steps toward reserved slot proposal. A mix of lab bench numbers and requests to run a P95-focused head-to-head.

Topics: benchmark deltas, tail latency, KV cache behavior, batching policy, fallback routing, dedicated vs hosted economics, security ask: KMS/audit log confirmation.

[00:00] Jordan Park: hey everyone, thanks for joining. uh so this is our weekly convergence standup for the pilot. maya and i will run through the bench snapshot, call out the deltas versus what you saw with IncumbentCloudAI, and then align on who's doing what for next week.

[00:18] Carlos Mendez: great, jordan, thanks. quick note — i'm on a weird connection so if audio cuts, i'll pop back in. overall looking for concrete tail-latency numbers, and whether the dedicated slot option buys us the 95p improvement we need.

[00:33] Maya Singh: yep. quick context: last week's run used our default quant profile q4_8 and standard batching (max batch 32, micro-batch 8). we also turned on prefix KV caching for session warm calls. the incumbent baseline was measured using their managed endpoint with similar concurrent clients (20 concurrent streams).

[01:02] Priya Kapoor: real quick — when you say prefix KV caching, is that the same as your "KV cache" optimization? in our notes some folks called it "KV cash" earlier, so wanted to confirm.

[01:10] Maya Singh: yes that's our KV cache — sorry about the mis-typo on earlier doc. it keeps the KV for repeated prefixes so subsequent tokens skip recompute. helps a lot for chat-style persistence.

[01:30] Jordan Park: ok maya, can you run through the numbers from Monday's lab? and please call out p50/p95/p99 if you have them.

[01:38] Maya Singh: sure. so aggregated across the 6 hour bench: Redwood hosted variant (rwd-v1-q4_8) median per-token latency was about 12ms p50, p95 62ms, p99 145ms. throughput per GPU for the workload profile averaged ~1850 tokens/sec at steady state. IncumbentCloudAI from our comparative run: p50 14ms, p95 110ms, p99 260ms, throughput ~1600 tokens/sec. so delta is mostly in the tail — we see ~40-45% improvement at p95 vs incumbent and ~44% better throughput.

[02:20] Carlos Mendez: hmm those p95 numbers look promising. what's the variance across sequences? our production has bursts of long completions (1k-2k tokens). do these runs include longer sequences?

[02:34] Maya Singh: good flag — this run focused on 512 token sequences with a tail at 1024, not full 2k. we did a synthetic long-seq trial: for 2k sequences p95 on Redwood was 220ms vs incumbent 430ms, so still a tail improvement but absolute latency grows as expected.

[03:00] Priya Kapoor: were KV cache warm hits accounted for in the head-to-head? i.e., incumbent might not have prefix caching in their config.

[03:10] Maya Singh: in the primary run we enabled prefix caching on both sides where possible; with incumbent their caching behavior is not identical — some of their sessions didn't persist KV the same way, so there are small differences. that's why one of the next steps is to run a canonical prompt set with an identical warm/cold split to be sure.

[03:33] Sofia Lane: also curious about batching tradeoffs — our concern is reducing p95 without increasing median much; what batching knobs give us that?

[03:44] Maya Singh: we looked at two knobs: aggressive batching (bigger max batch) increases throughput but can widen tail if you hit tail spikes; dynamic batching with target latency cutoffs helps keep tail down. for this workload, moving max batch from 32 to 16 cut p95 by ~12% while throughput dropped ~7%.

[04:10] Jordan Park: the routing piece is also important — if you go to our dedicated slots, you get guaranteed GPU isolation and that reduces tail from noisy neighbors. that's part of the reserved capacity value prop.

[04:22] Carlos Mendez: can you quantify that? what does dedicated buy us in p95 terms?

[04:28] Maya Singh: on our dedicated pool runs (reserved 3x A800-equivalent slots), p95 dropped from 62ms to ~48ms for the 512 token workload — roughly 23% improvement in p95 versus hosted shared pools under load. throughput remained comparable.

[04:50] Priya Kapoor: ok so dedicated helps. what about cost delta? incumbents are giving us a certain unit cost — i need to see the math if dedicated will be within our budget.

[04:59] Jordan Park: i'll send the reserved slot pricing and a side-by-side cost-per-1M-tokens estimate — includes amortized slot cost and expected utilization. that's one of the next steps.

[05:14] Maya Singh: one more bench note — we saw a particular regression when quantization profile q3_6 was used; p99 increased substantially for longer sequences due to extra decode overhead. q4_8 is a safer default for tail-sensitive workloads.

[05:34] Priya Kapoor: interesting. so you'd recommend q4_8 for our prod rollout?

[05:39] Maya Singh: yes for now. once we have the production sample we can tune to q3_6 for cost if the tail isn't a hard blocker.

[05:50] Jordan Park: let's talk about fallback and routing playbook. if a slot is saturated or a region degradation happens, we can automically route to a cheaper variant that maintains logits parity but may be slightly slower. we can configure thresholds — e.g., if p95 > 250ms in region, route 15% to fallback.

[06:12] Carlos Mendez: that sounds sensible — question is whether the fallback affects determinism for us. for financial transcripts we have to keep output stability.

[06:22] Maya Singh: fallback variants are deterministic given the same model weights and temp settings; differences come from architecture/quantization. we can pin model version and keep a canary to validate diffs with your eval set before ramping.

[06:38] Sofia Lane: on security — we had a couple of questions in the thread about KMS integration and audit logs for inference calls. are those ready for us to review?

[06:47] Jordan Park: yes — Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and we emit per-request audit logs with token usage and model id. i'll attach the security pack after this call. if anything is missing we'll schedule a dedicated security review.

[07:05] Priya Kapoor: good. also SSO integration — SAML support? we want RBAC on deployment configs.

[07:12] Jordan Park: SAML SSO + SCIM provisioning supported for the console. RBAC at org/project/model level also available. i'll include the specific docs when i share the security pack.

[07:24] Maya Singh: back to bench: we ran a short endurance (6 hr soak) with burst traffic and observed that incumbent's 99th percentile drifted up during hour 4 and 5 — likely noisy neighbor or GC on their infra; Redwood run stayed steadier. i'll share the time-series plots.

[07:44] Carlos Mendez: can we get the raw logs or at least the summarized csv so our SREs can plug into our observability?

[07:50] Jordan Park: yes, we'll share the bench csv and a dashboard link. mindful of redactions — but we'll provide anonymized traces, token counts, latency histograms.

[08:03] Priya Kapoor: i want to push on one thing — your throughput numbers look great, but our production mix has many short queries and occasional very long queries. what's impact on batching policies when the queue is dominated by short queries?

[08:18] Maya Singh: short queries reduce batch efficiency, but our continuous batching pipeline prioritizes latency SLOs: if short queries are latency-sensitive we can set a lower max wait (ms) before dispatch so they don't sit. that reduces throughput slightly but keeps tail in control. we have policies per-route to tailor this.

[08:40] Sofia Lane: any talk on model variants? if we quantize more aggressively for non-critical routes is that supported?

[08:47] Jordan Park: yes — per-route model variant selection is supported; you can send a route to higher-q or lower-q model. Redwood Console can show unit-cost delta per-route so you can make tradeoffs.

[08:59] Carlos Mendez: ok great. so what's the canonical next bench we should run so everyone's aligned?

[09:06] Maya Singh: propose: canonical prompt set (we'll use your prod-sample once uploaded) with 30% long sequences (1k–2k), 70% short (under 128). warm/cold split 60/40. run for 6 hours under 20 concurrent clients. capture p50/p95/p99 and throughput per-GPU. compare Redwood hosted, Redwood dedicated (reserved 3 slots), and IncumbentCloudAI baseline.

[09:32] Priya Kapoor: that sounds good. i'll upload the sample and annotate the SLOs.

[09:40] Jordan Park: perfect. recap on deliverables — maya runs the head-to-head with those params and shares results as CSV and dashboard, jordan sends pricing + security pack, salix shares sample. then we reconvene next week same time.

[09:55] Carlos Mendez: a quick note on procurement — if the numbers look good we'll want a 60-day PO timeline; can you accommodate reserved capacity start dates?

[10:03] Jordan Park: yes we can align start dates; i'll get with our CS/finance crew once you confirm expected start month.

[10:12] Priya Kapoor: final thing — can you also include an example eval script we can run against your canary to validate semantic parity?

[10:18] Maya Singh: yes we'll include an eval harness (python notebook + metrics) for exact-match, ROUGE-like and embedding-similarity checks. we'll include threshold suggestions.

[10:30] Jordan Park: awesome. thanks all. we'll follow up with the artifacts and the action items noted. talk next week.

[10:35] (call ends)

Notes about transcript: occasional misattribution and filler words preserved. Some proper nouns may be slightly off (e.g., "KV cash" heard in early notes). Links referenced during call: bench csv (link shared privately), reserved slot proposal (to be attached).
